title: Mei Lanfang in Moscow, 1930–1935
subtitle: A Peking opera company on Broadway and in Hollywood, then in Moscow and Leningrad, and the discussion of 14 April 1935
intro: In the spring of 1935 the most famous actor in China played to Soviet audiences for about a month. Mei Lanfang (Mei Lan-fang in the older romanisation, 1894–1961) was a dan, a male performer of women's roles in jingju, the theatre Western audiences called Peking opera. He travelled at the invitation of VOKS, the All-Union Society for Cultural Relations with Foreign Countries. His company of about two dozen performers and musicians sailed from Shanghai in late February on a Soviet steamer and crossed Siberia by the Far Eastern Express. They reached Moscow on 12 March, played there and in Leningrad, and gave a farewell performance at the Bolshoi on 13 April. On 14 April VOKS held a closed discussion of what the visit had shown. The directors Vsevolod Meyerhold and Alexander Tairov, the film-maker Sergei Eisenstein and the writer Sergei Tretyakov were among the people in Moscow that spring who wrote and spoke about him. Konstantin Stanislavsky, the most famous of them, stayed away from the public events. So were two foreigners, Edward Gordon Craig and Bertolt Brecht.

The prologue is the American tour of 1930. Mei's advisers, the dramatist Qi Rushan (Ch'i Ju-shan) and the Nankai University theatre man Zhang Pengchun (Chang P'eng-ch'un, known in English as P. C. Chang), had spent years preparing it. They cut the plays to Western lengths, wrote English programmes and had illustrations of hand gestures and costumes drawn. The company opened on Broadway at the 49th Street Theatre on 17 February 1930 and moved to the larger National Theatre in March. It then played Chicago, San Francisco, Los Angeles and Honolulu. In Los Angeles Mei met Charlie Chaplin, and the University of Southern California and Pomona College gave him honorary doctorates. Eisenstein, who was in Hollywood that summer, later wrote that he first heard of Mei from Chaplin.

The record is not a set of diaries. It is press articles dated by their issues (Tretyakov's pieces in Pravda, Eisenstein's in Komsomolskaya Pravda, the Shanghai and Tianjin dailies), programme essays, one letter (Marianne Moore's), the dated notebooks Craig called daybooks, the minutes of the 14 April meeting, and recollections that Mei and his deputy director Yu Shangyuan wrote down years later. The chapter tags each source by its form. The memoirs are marked as written later, because some of their best-known stories, above all Stanislavsky's praise, cannot be matched to anything written in 1935.

Two later inventions grew around the meeting of 14 April. In 1986 the Swedish Slavist Lars Kleberg staged a play in Kraków that imagined the discussion, with Brecht and Craig among the speakers. A French production directed by Antoine Vitez followed at Avignon in 1988 as 'Les Apprentis sorciers'. A Chinese translation then circulated in 1988 as if it were a record of what had been said. Kleberg later found the real stenographic minutes in the former Central State Archive of the October Revolution and published them in Russian in Iskusstvo kino (1992). A Chinese version appeared in Zhonghua xiqu in 1993. Secondary accounts of those minutes say that Vladimir Nemirovich-Danchenko chaired and that Tretyakov, Meyerhold and Eisenstein were among about thirty people who spoke or took part. They do not record Brecht or Erwin Piscator as speakers. Stanislavsky was not there. Accounts differ on Craig: his daybook has an entry for 14 April, but one Chinese account says the foreign guests were not on the invitation list. The chapter reports these positions without settling them. It does not quote the minutes.

The visit was also diplomacy. China and the Soviet Union had restored relations in December 1932, and the Chinese ambassador Yan Huiqing (W. W. Yen) travelled on the same ship. So did the film star Hu Die (Hu Tieh), on her way to the Moscow film festival. The Foreign Commissariat approved the speeches. The visit came three months after the murder of Kirov and as the doctrine of socialist realism was being pressed on the theatres. Soviet critics argued over whether Mei's conventions were a lesson in realism or a defence of the 'formalism' that Meyerhold was accused of. Within five years several of the hosts were dead. VOKS's chairman Alexander Arosev, Karl Radek, who had written on Mei in Izvestia, and Tretyakov were arrested in 1937. Tretyakov was killed that year and Arosev in 1938. Meyerhold was arrested in June 1939 and shot on 2 February 1940. The chapter records these deaths as a coda and does not read them back into what was written in 1935.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian. Republican China used the Gregorian calendar with Minguo years (1930 = Minguo 19, 1935 = Minguo 24). Newspaper items are given by issue date, which is often the day after the event they report. Chinese and Soviet papers sometimes disagree: the Dagong bao gave 19 March for the Moscow premiere, Izvestia reported a preview on 22 March, and the first public performance is usually dated 23 March. Recollections written decades later carry the dates their authors gave and are marked approx.

eyes.name: Mei Lanfang (梅蘭芳; Mei Lan-fang)
eyes.role: Leading dan (female-role) actor of jingju, aged 35 in 1930 and 40 in 1935; head of his own company
eyes.side: Chinese performers; guest of VOKS in 1935
eyes.where: Peiping and Shanghai; on tour in the United States (1930) and the USSR (1935)
eyes.form: memoir (written later), interviews and speeches reported in the press
eyes.authenticity: No diary of either tour is known. Mei's accounts of 1935 come from speeches reported in the press and from recollections written in the 1950s, including the chapter on his first visit to the USSR and his friendship with Eisenstein, collected in 《我的電影生活》 (My Film Life, 1962). His stage memoir 《舞台生活四十年》 (Forty Years on Stage) was dictated to Xu Jichuan from 1950 and is also a later work. Both were written under the People's Republic and stress Soviet friendship.
eyes.bio: Mei rebuilt the dan repertoire after 1911 with new dances and costumes and became the best-known face of Chinese theatre abroad. He had played Japan in 1919 and 1924. He chose the American tour of 1930 and the Soviet tour of 1935 as tests of whether jingju could be understood without translation. His later recollections are the only source for some private meetings, which is why they are flagged.

sources.title: Janne Risum, 'The Foreign-Policy Aspect of Mei Lanfang's Soviet Tour in 1935', Nordic Theatre Studies
'Mei Lanfang and Stanislavsky: the deconstruction of an intercultural myth on the international stage', Theatre Research International

eyes.name: Qi Rushan (齊如山; Ch'i Ju-shan)
eyes.role: Dramatist, theatre historian and Mei's chief adviser; aged 54 in 1930
eyes.where: Peiping; with the company in the United States, 1930
eyes.vantage_label: the adviser who prepared the 1930 tour
eyes.authenticity: His account of the American tour, 《梅蘭芳遊美記》 (Mei Lanfang's American Tour), appeared in Peiping in 1933. It is a narrative written after the event, not a day-by-day journal. He also wrote many of Mei's new plays and much later memoirs in Taiwan.
eyes.bio: Qi was a gentleman scholar who had travelled in Europe and turned to the theatre. For years before 1930 he and Mei's backers prepared the American tour, choosing plays, compiling explanatory material and arranging drawings of gestures and costumes. His book is the insider's account of how the tour was built.

sources.title: Rising Tide Foundation: Mei Lanfang's Tour of America (long account drawing on 1930 New York Times reports)
Asian American History NYC: #24 On Broadway

eyes.name: Zhang Pengchun (張彭春; Chang P'eng-ch'un; P. C. Chang)
eyes.role: Professor and theatre director at Nankai University, Tianjin; director of the 1930 American tour (aged 37) and chief director of the 1935 Soviet tour
eyes.where: Tianjin; New York and the American tour, 1930; Moscow and Leningrad, 1935
eyes.vantage_label: tour director and interpreter of the stage to foreigners
eyes.form: press reports and interviews; later accounts by others
eyes.authenticity: His part in both tours is documented in press reports and the accounts of colleagues. Nankai gave him two months' leave in 1935. No personal diary of either tour is cited in the sources used here.
eyes.bio: A Columbia-trained educator and stage director who had staged Ibsen and Molière at Nankai, Zhang explained jingju to American audiences in 1930. He visited the USSR in 1931 and directed the 1935 tour. After the war he became vice-chairman of the UN Commission on Human Rights and one of the drafters of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, adopted on 10 December 1948.

sources.title: Aisixiang: the 1935 tour, Tretyakov, Zhang Pengchun and Eisenstein's filming
Rising Tide Foundation: Mei Lanfang's Tour of America (long account drawing on 1930 New York Times reports)

eyes.name: Yu Shangyuan (余上沅; Yü Shang-yüan)
eyes.role: Dramatist and theatre educator; deputy director of the 1935 tour, aged 37
eyes.where: Moscow and Leningrad, 1935; then on to Europe with Mei
eyes.authenticity: Yu's account of Mei's meeting with Stanislavsky is one of the two main sources for that meeting. It was written after the event, and the scholars cited here could not match it to a Soviet record of 1935 beyond a newspaper notice.
eyes.bio: Yu had studied theatre at Carnegie Tech and Columbia and helped found the 'national drama' movement of the 1920s. In 1935 he was founding head of the National Drama School in Nanjing. He went to Moscow as the professional theatre man beside Zhang, watching rehearsal and staging methods as well as the company's reception.

sources.title: 'Mei Lanfang and Stanislavsky: the deconstruction of an intercultural myth on the international stage', Theatre Research International
Renmin zhengxie wang (2019): Mei Lanfang's 1935 visit, the 14 April discussion and the Kleberg play

eyes.name: Hu Die (胡蝶; Hu Tieh, 'Butterfly Wu')
eyes.role: Film actress, voted Shanghai's 'Movie Queen' in 1933; aged 26; delegate to the Moscow film festival
eyes.side: Chinese film delegation travelling with the ambassador and Mei's company
eyes.where: On the Soviet steamer and the Trans-Siberian, then Moscow, then western Europe
eyes.authenticity: Her travel book of the 1935 journey, usually cited as 《胡蝶女士歐遊雜記》 (Miss Hu Die's Notes on a European Journey, Shanghai, 1935), is a published narrative and has not been checked here. Her presence at the VOKS banquet of 14 March is reported by Shenbao.
eyes.bio: The best-known Chinese film actress of the early sound era went to the Moscow International Film Festival of February–March 1935 and arrived after much of it was over. She travelled with Mei. Moscow crowds who had never seen him out of makeup reportedly took her for the famous 'actress' Mei Lanfang.

sources.title: Soviet and Chinese press of 1935 on the tour (Pravda, Izvestia, Shenbao, Dagong bao), Vestnik, Yaroslavl State Pedagogical University, 2025 no. 3, pp. 228–241

eyes.name: Sergei Tretyakov
eyes.role: Writer and dramatist, aged 42; author of the play 'Roar, China!' and VOKS's guide to the company
eyes.where: Moscow; met the train on its way into the city
eyes.vantage_label: host and press voice of the visit
eyes.authenticity: His Pravda articles of 12, 14, 18 and 26 March 1935 are listed by date in the 2025 Vestnik study. They are newspaper pieces, not private writing.
eyes.bio: Tretyakov had taught Russian in Beijing in 1924–25 and his 'Roar, China!' had been staged by Meyerhold and in Shanghai. He was the Soviet writer who knew China best and Brecht's friend and translator. He was arrested in July 1937 and killed in custody later that year. He was rehabilitated in 1956.

sources.title: Soviet and Chinese press of 1935 on the tour (Pravda, Izvestia, Shenbao, Dagong bao), Vestnik, Yaroslavl State Pedagogical University, 2025 no. 3, pp. 228–241
Aisixiang: the 1935 tour, Tretyakov, Zhang Pengchun and Eisenstein's filming

eyes.name: Sergei Eisenstein
eyes.role: Film director and theorist, aged 37; member of the VOKS reception committee
eyes.form: articles and programme essay dated by publication; film footage
eyes.authenticity: His article in Komsomolskaya Pravda (12 March 1935), his programme essay known as 'The Enchanter from the Pear Garden' and an English version in International Literature no. 5 (1935) survive. The fuller text was published in the USSR only in 1968. Of the sound footage he shot of Mei, a short fragment survives.
eyes.bio: Eisenstein had travelled to Hollywood in 1930 and then spent 1930–32 in Mexico. He was the Soviet artist most interested in Chinese and Japanese stage conventions, which fed his ideas of montage. In 1935 he was being attacked at the cinema workers' conference in January for formalism, and he used the visit to film Mei.

sources.title: Eisenstein, 'Mei Lan-fang and the Chinese Theatre', International Literature no. 5 (1935), reposted text
Georges Banu, 'Mei Lanfang : procès et utopie de la scène occidentale', Jeu 49 (1988)

eyes.name: Vsevolod Meyerhold
eyes.role: Theatre director, aged 61; head of the Meyerhold Theatre
eyes.vantage_label: director in the audience and at the discussion
eyes.form: statements and speeches dated by publication or minutes
eyes.authenticity: His statement to Sovetskoe iskusstvo on the day of Mei's arrival and his speech of 14 April are known from the newspaper and the minutes. His 1936 remark on a coming union of Western and Chinese stage devices comes from a later lecture, cited by Min Tian.
eyes.bio: Meyerhold had used Asian stage conventions since before the Revolution. He saw in Mei a confirmation of his own biomechanics and his 'conventional' theatre at the moment those ideas were being condemned. His theatre was closed in 1938. He was arrested in June 1939 and shot on 2 February 1940.

sources.title: Min Tian, 'Meyerhold Meets Mei Lanfang: Staging the Grotesque and the Beautiful', Comparative Drama 33.2 (1999)
Haun Saussy, 'Mei Lanfang in Moscow, 1935: Familiar, Unfamiliar, Defamiliar', MCLC 18.1 (2006), abstract

eyes.name: Vladimir Nemirovich-Danchenko
eyes.role: Co-founder of the Moscow Art Theatre, aged 76
eyes.authenticity: His role as chairman is stated in the minutes as reported by Kleberg and in Chinese accounts. The text of the minutes is not quoted here.
eyes.bio: Stanislavsky's partner in founding the Moscow Art Theatre in 1898, Nemirovich-Danchenko was the senior figure of the Soviet stage in 1935. He opened and closed the discussion in which the younger directors argued over what Mei's art meant for Soviet theatre.

sources.title: China News Service (2023): the 1935 tour, the Bolshoi farewell and the 14 April symposium

eyes.name: Konstantin Stanislavsky
eyes.role: Co-founder of the Moscow Art Theatre, aged 72 and in poor health
eyes.side: Soviet hosts (named to the VOKS committee)
eyes.where: His house in Leontievsky Lane, Moscow
eyes.vantage_label: named host who stayed away from the public events
eyes.form: press notice; later recollections by others
eyes.authenticity: His name was proposed for the reception committee in a Foreign Commissariat memo of 2 February 1935. He was crossed off the lists of those at the VOKS luncheon and the 14 April discussion. The Moscow Daily News reported on 1 April 1935 that Mei had visited him. His often-quoted praise of Mei rests on Mei's essays of 1953 and later, and on Yu Shangyuan; no record of it from 1935 has been found.
eyes.bio: Stanislavsky rarely went out in 1935 and worked at home. Chinese writing on Mei since the 1950s has paired the two as the great realist and the great conventional actor. A study in Theatre Research International traces how that pairing was built after the event.

sources.title: 'Mei Lanfang and Stanislavsky: the deconstruction of an intercultural myth on the international stage', Theatre Research International

eyes.name: Edward Gordon Craig
eyes.role: English stage designer and theorist, aged 62, living in Italy
eyes.authenticity: His Daybook VIII, with entries for 2, 14, 16 and 18 April 1935, and his annotated copy of the Moscow programme 'Mei Lan-Fang and the Chinese Theatre' are at the Harry Ransom Center, Austin. Min Tian used them in 2007. The entries' content is reported only in paraphrase.
eyes.bio: Craig had designed the Moscow Art Theatre's Hamlet with Stanislavsky in 1911–12 and had argued for decades that the actor should become a disciplined 'über-marionette'. In Moscow in 1935 he found in Mei a living example of the trained, controlled actor he had argued for. He wrote about the visit in 'Some Weeks in Moscow' (Drama, 1935) and 'The Russian Theatre To-Day' (London Mercury, 1935).

sources.title: Min Tian, 'Gordon Craig, Mei Lanfang and the Chinese Theatre', Theatre Research International 32.2 (2007)

eyes.name: Bertolt Brecht
eyes.role: German playwright in exile in Denmark, aged 37
eyes.vantage_label: foreign spectator who turned what he saw into theory
eyes.form: essay manuscripts and letters (dated by publication and correspondence)
eyes.authenticity: A short text, 'Bemerkungen über die chinesische Schauspielkunst', was sent by Steffin to Walter Benjamin in September 1935. The longer essay appeared first in English as 'The Fourth Wall of China', translated by Eric Walter White, in Life and Letters To-day (Winter 1936). No German source text for that translation has been found. The German 'Verfremdungseffekte in der chinesischen Schauspielkunst' was published only in 1957. He is not recorded as speaking at the 14 April discussion.
eyes.bio: Brecht stayed in Moscow with Tretyakov's help and saw Mei perform, apparently while ill with flu. His essay used Mei's way of showing a character from the outside to define the 'alienation effect'. Scholars still argue over how much he took from Mei and how much from Tretyakov and the Russian Formalists' idea of making the familiar strange.

sources.title: Brecht Guide (UW–Madison): 'The Fourth Wall of China', Life and Letters To-day 15.6 (Winter 1936)
'Verfremdungseffekt or Entfremdungseffekt: A Study of Brecht's Manuscripts on Chinese Theatre', Theatre Survey

eyes.name: Marianne Moore
eyes.role: American poet and former editor of The Dial, aged 42
eyes.authenticity: Her letter to Monroe Wheeler of 18 March 1930 is in her published correspondence (Selected Letters, 1997) and is summarised in the Zurich China–West chronology.
eyes.bio: Moore saw a programme of four short plays by Mei's company during the New York run. Her letter is a private, dated response from an American writer who knew nothing of jingju beforehand. It stands beside the professional reviews.

sources.title: China–West chronology (University of Zurich): Marianne Moore on Mei Lanfang, 1930

eyes.name: Brooks Atkinson
eyes.role: Drama critic of the New York Times, aged 35
eyes.authenticity: His review after the opening and a longer Sunday column within the week are in the New York Times archive. They were published after 1928 and are summarised, not quoted.
eyes.bio: Atkinson was the most influential theatre critic in New York. His praise helped turn a two-week booking into five. In 1942–44, as the Times correspondent in Chongqing, he wrote on China's war and politics.

sources.title: Asian American History NYC: #24 On Broadway
Rising Tide Foundation: Mei Lanfang's Tour of America (long account drawing on 1930 New York Times reports)

entries.headline: Ten years of preparation packed into crates
entries.digest: Qi Rushan's account describes the last stage of a plan he and Mei's backers had worked on since the 1910s. Plays were cut to fit Western evenings. English programmes were written, and drawings of costumes, instruments and hand gestures were prepared for American audiences. The company sailed from Shanghai at the turn of the year for the Pacific crossing.
entries.source_note: Qi Rushan, 梅蘭芳遊美記 (1933), as summarised in the Rising Tide account, which gives the departure as late December 1929; other accounts give January 1930.

entries.headline: The company steps off the train in Manhattan
entries.digest: After the Pacific crossing and the train east, Mei's company reached New York's Grand Central Terminal. A private performance in Washington followed on 14 February, arranged by the Chinese minister. The New York press had been primed for weeks with stories about the man who played women.
entries.source_note: Rising Tide account, citing New York Times reports of February 1930.

entries.headline: Broadway opening at the 49th Street Theatre
entries.digest: Mei opened on Broadway. Each short play was introduced in English by a mistress of ceremonies, and printed explanations were handed out. The run was booked for two weeks. Demand forced an extension and on 3 March a move to the larger National Theatre. Some accounts give 16 February for the opening.
entries.source_note: IBDB production record (opening 17 Feb, 41 performances, closing 22 Mar); Chinafile/Caixin and Rising Tide give 17 February.

entries.headline: Zhang Pengchun explains the stage to Americans
entries.digest: Zhang served as the tour's director and its interpreter to the American public. He spoke to audiences and the press about the conventions they were seeing: the bare stage, the symbolic props, the role types. His Columbia training and fluent English made him the bridge between the company and the critics.
entries.source_note: Rising Tide and Smithsonian accounts of Zhang's role; exact dates of his talks not checked.

entries.headline: The Times critic gives way to grace
entries.digest: Atkinson reviewed the opening. He described an art whose conventions were foreign to New York but whose chief impression was grace, stateliness and imagination. Within the week he followed with a longer column on the same performances.
entries.source_note: New York Times review after opening night and Sunday follow-up, as described in the Rising Tide and Baruch accounts; exact issue dates not checked.

entries.place: National Theatre, West 41st Street, New York
entries.headline: The run moves to a bigger house
entries.digest: With tickets being resold at several times face value, the engagement transferred to the National Theatre for three more weeks. Mei became a social attraction as well as a theatrical one, with luncheons, a newspaper ball and a tulip named after him at a flower show.
entries.source_note: IBDB (National Theatre 3–22 March 1930); Rising Tide for the social calendar.

entries.headline: A poet overwhelmed by the female roles
entries.digest: Moore wrote to her friend Monroe Wheeler that she had seen a programme of four short plays by Mei's company. She said she had been overwhelmed by his playing of women's roles. The letter is a private response from a writer who had come to the theatre knowing little of what she would see.
entries.source_note: Letter to Monroe Wheeler, 18 March 1930, Selected Letters of Marianne Moore (1997); summarised in the University of Zurich China–West chronology.

entries.headline: Last New York night, then west
entries.digest: The New York engagement closed after 41 performances and a farewell dinner at the Ambassador Hotel followed. The company went on to Chicago for two weeks and reached San Francisco by mid-April. There it played thirteen days in three theatres, and the city's Chinese community gave banquets in its honour.
entries.source_note: IBDB closing date; Rising Tide for Chicago and San Francisco; Calisphere photograph of the San Francisco banquet.

entries.headline: Hollywood: Chaplin, Pickford and Fairbanks
entries.digest: In Los Angeles the company played twelve days at the Philharmonic Auditorium in May and June. Mei met Charlie Chaplin, Mary Pickford and Douglas Fairbanks, and photographs of him with Chaplin were widely printed.
entries.source_note: Smithsonian Magazine and USC Today accounts of the meetings; Rising Tide for the Philharmonic Auditorium engagement. No exact day for the Chaplin meeting has been confirmed.

entries.headline: Eisenstein hears of Mei from Chaplin
entries.digest: Eisenstein arrived in Hollywood in 1930 on his contract with Paramount and became friendly with Chaplin. In his 1935 article he wrote that it was Chaplin who first told him about Mei Lanfang. Within months he left for Mexico to make the film that became 'Que viva México!'.
entries.source_note: Eisenstein, 'Mei Lan-fang and the Chinese Theatre', International Literature no. 5 (1935), opening paragraph.

entries.headline: USC makes the actor a doctor
entries.digest: At the University of Southern California's 47th commencement Mei was among the honorary graduates, alongside the singer Margaret Matzenauer and the songwriter Carrie Jacobs Bond. Pomona College in Claremont had already given him an honorary doctorate at a ceremony it rearranged for him.
entries.source_note: USC commencement programme, 7 June 1930 (Calisphere); Time, 23 June 1930. The Pomona date was not confirmed.

entries.headline: Home after Honolulu
entries.digest: After twelve more days of performances in Honolulu, Mei arrived back in Shanghai. The New York Times ran the dispatch the next day. The tour had lasted about seven months.
entries.source_note: New York Times, 20 July 1930, as cited in the Rising Tide account.

entries.headline: Qi publishes the story of the American tour
entries.digest: Qi's 梅蘭芳遊美記 set out the long planning, the choice of plays and the reception city by city. It was written as a record for Chinese readers of how the theatre had been explained to foreigners. It became the base for later accounts of the tour.
entries.source_note: Qi Rushan, 梅蘭芳遊美記 (Peiping, 1933), cited in the Rising Tide account; edition not seen.

entries.headline: A memo names Stanislavsky to greet Mei
entries.digest: A memo of the Second Eastern Department of the Foreign Commissariat proposed a reception committee for the visit. Arosev of VOKS and the Chinese ambassador would be co-chairs. Stanislavsky, Nemirovich-Danchenko, Meyerhold, Tairov, Eisenstein and Tretyakov were among the members. The Chinese government issued a parallel order on 6 February.
entries.source_note: Memo of 2 Feb 1935, in Russko-kitaiskie otnosheniya vol. III, pp. 388–389, as cited in the 2025 Vestnik study.

entries.headline: Briefing on the Soviet stage before sailing
entries.digest: Zhang met the playwright Tian Han at the Xinya hotel to talk over the Soviet repertoire and theatres he was about to see. Nankai had given him two months' leave to be the tour's chief director. The day before, more than 500 guests had attended a tea in Shanghai to see off the ambassador and Mei.
entries.source_note: Aisixiang article on the 1935 tour; Dagong bao, 19 Feb 1935, as cited in the 2025 Vestnik study.

entries.headline: Sailing north on a Soviet steamer
entries.digest: The company of about two dozen left Shanghai on a steamer sent by the Soviet government, usually named as the Severny. Shenbao had reported on 8 February that they would go by a special Russian ship via Vladivostok. Ambassador Yan Huiqing and the film delegation with Hu Die were on board. At Vladivostok the diplomats and artists separated, and the company crossed Siberia by the Far Eastern Express.
entries.source_note: Shenbao, 8 Feb 1935 (via the 2025 Vestnik study); China News Service, 2023 (tour 21 Feb–21 Apr); Risum, Nordic Theatre Studies, on the Vladivostok parting. The ship's name was not confirmed in a 1935 source.

entries.place: At sea and on the Trans-Siberian
entries.headline: A film star on the long way to Moscow
entries.digest: Hu Die travelled to the Moscow film festival with the same party. The sea leg and the long train journey meant the Chinese delegation reached Moscow as the festival was ending. Her travel book of the year describes the journey and the European cities that followed.
entries.source_note: Travel account 胡蝶女士歐遊雜記 (1935), not seen; festival timing from general accounts.

entries.place: On the Far Eastern Express outside Moscow; Pravda
entries.headline: Tretyakov boards the train before Moscow
entries.digest: Tretyakov went out to meet the express before it reached the capital. He described the arrival of a 24-member company under the hot lights of the newsreel cameras. The same day Pravda printed his welcome article presenting Mei as 'our guest'. Izvestia ran B. A. Vasiliev's introduction to Chinese theatre.
entries.source_note: Tretyakov, Pravda, 12 and 14 March 1935; Vasiliev, Izvestia, 12 March 1935 (2025 Vestnik study).

entries.headline: Arrival after nearly twenty days on the road
entries.digest: Mei reached Moscow by the Far Eastern Express after almost three weeks of travel. Posters and shop windows in Moscow and Leningrad had been announcing him since late February. VOKS had printed three Russian books on him and on Chinese theatre for the occasion. Ambassador Yan arrived the following day.
entries.source_note: Pravda, 14 March 1935; Renmin zhengxie wang (2019); Risum (arrival one day before Yan, who arrived 13 March).

entries.headline: Eisenstein writes a welcome in the youth daily
entries.digest: Eisenstein's article appeared in Komsomolskaya Pravda as the company arrived. He met Mei from the first day and soon proposed filming him. His longer essay for the VOKS programme read Chinese theatre as a model for the unity of sound, movement and image he sought in sound film.
entries.source_note: Eisenstein, Komsomolskaya Pravda, 12 March 1935 (2025 Vestnik study); Banu, Jeu 49 (1988).

entries.headline: Meyerhold praises the man who plays women
entries.digest: On the day of Mei's arrival Meyerhold told the arts paper Sovetskoe iskusstvo that a man playing a woman was the highest form of theatrical convention. It was a provocative claim to make as socialist realism was being promoted. He went on to attend the performances and the closing discussion.
entries.source_note: Statement reported in the dissertation text at core.ac.uk (download 352201808); issue date given only as the day of arrival.

entries.headline: Banquet with the ambassadors
entries.digest: VOKS gave a banquet for the guests. Arosev welcomed them, Ambassador Yan and the Soviet ambassador to China, Dmitri Bogomolov, attended, and Hu Die sat among the Chinese party. Yan said in his speech that beside Mei he felt like a supporting actor. Shenbao reported the dinner two days later.
entries.source_note: Shenbao, 16 March 1935 (2025 Vestnik study); Risum, Nordic Theatre Studies, p. 96, on Yan's speech.

entries.headline: 'Mei Lanfang in Moscow': a guide for Soviet readers
entries.digest: Tretyakov's second Pravda piece described the company's first days in the city. He set out for readers who had never seen Chinese theatre what to look for. Four days later he wrote on the stage decorations and costumes the company had brought.
entries.source_note: Tretyakov, Pravda, 14 and 18 March 1935 (2025 Vestnik study).

entries.headline: Mei watches Tairov's 'Egyptian Nights'
entries.digest: Mei visited the exhibition of seventeen years of Soviet theatre design and in the evening saw the Kamerny Theatre's 'Egyptian Nights', which drew on Shakespeare, Shaw and Pushkin. Tairov received him afterwards. It was the first of many evenings on which Mei was the spectator.
entries.source_note: Pravda, 16 March 1935 (2025 Vestnik study).

entries.place: Moscow (Great Hall of the Conservatory, as usually given)
entries.headline: First public performance in Moscow
entries.digest: After a preview for invited guests on 22 March, which Izvestia reported, the company gave its first public performance. The programme included 'The Fisherman's Revenge', in which an oar and footwork make the boat, and 'Rainbow Pass'. The same day Karl Radek published an article in Izvestia on old China speaking of the new. By 30 March Pravda counted seven performances and twelve thousand spectators.
entries.source_note: Risum, p. 97 (23 March); Izvestia, 23 March 1935 (preview on 22nd, and Radek article); Dagong bao gave 19 March; Pravda, 30 March 1935.

entries.headline: Brecht, with flu, goes to see Mei
entries.digest: Brecht had come from Denmark with Margarete Steffin and stayed in Moscow into the spring. Though ill, he went to the performances. He noted with irritation that most Soviet spectators reacted to Mei's death scenes with the same fellow-feeling as a European audience. He was more interested in how Mei showed his characters as an observer of them.
entries.source_note: Aisixiang article (Brecht ill with flu); Theatre Survey study of the manuscripts (his complaint about spectators); dates of attendance not established.

entries.headline: 'A new theatre of old forms'
entries.digest: In his fourth Pravda article Tretyakov argued that Mei's art was a living tradition being reformed from within. That line of argument suited the hour, because it let Soviet readers admire convention without calling it formalism. Igor Bachelis's review in Komsomolskaya Pravda two days earlier had made similar points.
entries.source_note: Tretyakov, Pravda, 26 March 1935; Bachelis, Komsomolskaya Pravda, 24 March 1935 (2025 Vestnik study).

entries.headline: Eisenstein asks to make a sound film
entries.digest: Eisenstein asked Mei to let him film a short sound picture for distribution across the Soviet Union. They chose the spear duel and dance of Lady Dongfang and Wang Bodang from 'Rainbow Pass' because it moved well on screen. Shooting was set for two days later.
entries.source_note: Aisixiang article, drawing on Mei's recollections and Chinese press.

entries.headline: A long night filming 'Rainbow Pass'
entries.digest: Eisenstein filmed scenes from two of the plays in a long session. Pravda reported the filming the next day. Tretyakov was at the studio and suggested a photograph, which shows him with Mei and Eisenstein. About two minutes of the footage are known to survive.
entries.source_note: Pravda, 30 March 1935 (2025 Vestnik study); Banu, Jeu 49 (29 March); Aisixiang article (Tretyakov at the shoot); HKW material on surviving footage.

entries.headline: Playing to a camera instead of a house
entries.digest: Mei described the shoot years later, in a chapter on his first Soviet visit and his friendship with Eisenstein. In his account the film was meant as a record of a stage art for audiences who could never see it live. The chapter was written in the 1950s and published with his other memories of film.
entries.source_note: Mei, 'First Visit to the Soviet Union and Friendship with Eisenstein', in 我的電影生活 (1962), cited by Risum; written later.

entries.headline: A newspaper reports Mei's visit to Stanislavsky
entries.digest: The English-language Moscow Daily News reported that Mei had called on Stanislavsky. Stanislavsky had been invited to the VOKS luncheon in mid-March but did not come, and his name was later crossed off the lists of those at VOKS events. What was said at the meeting comes only from Mei and Yu Shangyuan, writing later.
entries.source_note: Moscow Daily News, 1 April 1935, and VOKS lists, as cited in the Theatre Research International study of the Stanislavsky myth.

entries.headline: Yu's account of the old master's advice
entries.digest: Yu later described the visit. In his account Stanislavsky said that a good actor needs strict study of theory and technique and must also test himself before audiences, and he praised the free yet ordered movement of Mei's acting. Chinese writers later quoted versions of that praise that differ from each other. A study of the archives argues that the story grew in the 1950s.
entries.source_note: Yu Shangyuan's recollection, cited in the Theatre Research International study; Renmin zhengxie wang (2019) for the advice as Mei recalled it. Flagged as later recollection.

entries.headline: Leningrad: banquet and four nights
entries.digest: The company had left Moscow on 31 March and arrived in Leningrad on 1 April. More than a hundred guests attended a banquet on the 2nd, and four performances were planned for 2–5 April. On 4 April the bill was 'Fei Zhen'e and the Tiger General' and 'The Fisherman's Revenge'. Pravda announced that a farewell performance would be given at the Bolshoi on the return.
entries.source_note: Pravda, 30 March and 2 April 1935; Shenbao, 3 and 5 April 1935 (2025 Vestnik study).

entries.headline: Craig's daybook: Moscow in April
entries.digest: Craig recorded his Moscow weeks in his daybook. During these weeks he also studied the VOKS programme on Mei, marking passages in its essays and adding his own notes. His interest was in the training and discipline that let the actor control every gesture.
entries.source_note: Daybook VIII, entry for 2 April 1935, and annotated programme, Harry Ransom Center, as cited by Min Tian (2007); content reported only in paraphrase.

entries.headline: Farewell at the Bolshoi until three in the morning
entries.digest: The extra farewell performance at the Bolshoi ran until about three in the morning. Accounts say the audience called Mei back for eighteen curtain calls. It was the largest house of the tour and the last time the Soviet public saw him until the 1950s.
entries.source_note: Bakhrushin Theatre Museum page; China News Service, 2023.

entries.headline: Nemirovich-Danchenko chairs the closing discussion
entries.digest: VOKS held a closed discussion of Mei's art the day before the company left Moscow. Nemirovich-Danchenko, the senior director in the room, chaired it. A stenographer took it down. Mei himself learned only years later that minutes existed. About thirty Soviet theatre and film people took part.
entries.source_note: China News Service (2023); Renmin zhengxie wang (2019); Kleberg, Iskusstvo kino (1992) and 'The Story of a Stenogramme', Balagan (1996).

entries.headline: Meyerhold imagines 'Boris Godunov' played Mei's way
entries.digest: Meyerhold gave the most provocative speech. He asked the room to imagine Pushkin's 'Boris Godunov' staged with Mei's methods and spoke of the precision of his hands. His argument was that Soviet actors should learn from Mei's discipline. It cut against the official preference for psychological realism.
entries.source_note: Renmin zhengxie wang (2019), drawing on the minutes; Min Tian, Comparative Drama (1999). Minutes not quoted.

entries.headline: Eisenstein: a task for Soviet scholars
entries.digest: Eisenstein argued that Chinese theatre had to be studied and analysed by Soviet scholars and critics, not just admired. He spoke of the unity of movement and sound he had seen in it and of its system of signs. His argument linked Mei's art to his own theory of montage.
entries.source_note: China News Service (2023), summarising the minutes.

entries.headline: Tretyakov's long speech
entries.digest: Tretyakov spoke at length about what the visit had shown and why Soviet theatre should take it seriously. He had organised much of the visit and drew on his years in China. Chinese accounts of the minutes single out his speech for its length.
entries.source_note: Aisixiang article; Kleberg's publication of the minutes as reported in secondary literature.

entries.headline: Craig's daybook on the day of the discussion
entries.digest: Craig wrote a daybook entry on 14 April, and Min Tian's study of Craig and Mei draws on it together with Kleberg's copy of the minutes. Accounts of whether Craig was in the room differ: one Chinese account says the foreign guests were not on the invitation list. Further daybook entries follow on 16 and 18 April.
entries.source_note: Daybook VIII, 14, 16 and 18 April 1935 (Harry Ransom Center), cited by Min Tian (2007); Renmin zhengxie wang (2019) for the contrary view.

entries.headline: Mei answers his critics
entries.digest: Mei attended and replied to the speakers. In 'My Film Life' he later described the discussion as the Soviet artists' verdict on Chinese theatre, held the day before he left Moscow. He wrote that he had never obtained a record of it. His account does not touch on the quarrel over formalism that ran under the praise.
entries.source_note: Mei's 1950s recollections, in 我的電影生活 (1962), as summarised in Renmin zhengxie wang (2019); written later.

entries.headline: On to Europe's theatres
entries.digest: After the Moscow farewell Mei, Yu and part of the company left for a study tour of European theatres, including Warsaw, Berlin, Paris and London. The musicians and most of the actors went home. Yu's role on that leg was to observe theatre schools and staging.
entries.source_note: China News Service (2023) gives 21 April as the end of the Soviet tour; the European itinerary is from general accounts and not checked day by day.

entries.headline: Eisenstein's essay goes out in English
entries.digest: International Literature, the Moscow journal of the revolutionary writers' international, printed Eisenstein's essay in English. It opens with Chaplin and a legend of 'living dolls'. It then sets out the role types, the symbolic props and the listening audience of the Chinese theatre. The fuller Russian text was published only in 1968.
entries.source_note: International Literature no. 5 (1935), text reposted 2026; HKW material for the 1968 Russian publication.

entries.headline: Craig reports to English readers
entries.digest: Craig published 'Some Weeks in Moscow' in the British Drama League's magazine Drama and 'The Russian Theatre To-Day' in The London Mercury. He wrote warmly of Mei's training and control. The articles give a sympathetic Western visitor's view of the Moscow theatre in 1935.
entries.source_note: Min Tian (2007), list of Craig's 1935 articles; exact issues not checked.

entries.headline: First notes on Chinese acting sent to Benjamin
entries.digest: Margarete Steffin sent Walter Benjamin in Paris Brecht's short text 'Remarks on Chinese Acting' and asked him to place it. Benjamin acknowledged it in October. It was not published until 1949. It is the earliest form of the argument Brecht developed over the next year.
entries.source_note: Theatre Survey study of Brecht's manuscripts.

entries.headline: 'The Fourth Wall of China' appears in English
entries.digest: The longer essay appeared first in English, translated by Eric Walter White for Life and Letters To-day. It argued that the Chinese actor shows that he knows he is being watched and looks at his own gestures with surprise, and that this distance could serve a critical, political theatre. The German text was not published until 1957, under the title that gave the world the term 'Verfremdungseffekt'.
entries.source_note: Brecht Guide record 02308 (Life and Letters To-day 15.6, Winter 1936, pp. 116–123); Theatre Survey study.

entries.headline: Meyerhold foresees a union of East and West
entries.digest: In a lecture of 1936 Meyerhold said that some union of the devices of Western and Chinese theatre was bound to come. He had already dedicated his revised staging of Griboyedov's 'Woe from Wit' to Mei. Within two years his theatre was closed, and in 1940 he was shot.
entries.source_note: Min Tian, Comparative Drama (1999); Banu, Jeu 49 (1988), for the dedication.

entries.headline: Mei puts Stanislavsky's praise in writing
entries.digest: Passing through Moscow again in 1953, Mei heard from the director Komissarzhevsky a story about Stanislavsky's admiration for him. After Stanislavsky's reputation became official doctrine in China, Mei wrote essays describing the old master's praise. These are the main source of the pairing of the two men, and of a quotation that appears in several different Chinese wordings.
entries.source_note: Theatre Research International study of the Stanislavsky myth; Banu, Jeu 49. Flagged as later recollection.

convergences.label: Broadway first night
convergences.note: The performer, his two architects and the critic who would judge them were in the same theatre. Qi and Zhang had built the evening as an explanation, with programmes, an English-speaking hostess and short plays. Atkinson wrote that he could not follow it and was won over anyway.

convergences.label: The New York run at its height
convergences.note: A critic's public verdict and a poet's private letter on the same run of performances. Both writers fixed on how exact his playing of women was. Moore saw it as precise observation and Atkinson as stateliness.

convergences.label: Arrival in Moscow
convergences.note: On one day Tretyakov boarded the train, Eisenstein's welcome appeared in the youth daily, and Meyerhold praised the art of the man who played women. Each host claimed Mei for his own cause: Tretyakov for a living tradition, Eisenstein for montage, Meyerhold for convention.

convergences.label: VOKS banquet
convergences.note: A diplomatic dinner, with Arosev and the two ambassadors making speeches and the film star at the table. Tretyakov's Pravda piece of the same morning was introducing Chinese theatre to Soviet readers.

convergences.label: Filming at Mosfilm
convergences.note: The one surviving film record of the tour was made in a single long session. Eisenstein saw a system of signs, Mei saw the strain of acting for a lens, and Tretyakov set up the photograph that shows all three.

convergences.label: The Stanislavsky visit
convergences.note: A newspaper notice of 1 April is the only contemporary record. Everything said at the meeting comes from Mei and Yu, writing later. The VOKS lists show that Stanislavsky stayed away from the public events.

convergences.label: The VOKS discussion
convergences.note: The day the room argued about what Mei meant for Soviet theatre. Meyerhold wanted his discipline, Eisenstein wanted it studied, and Tretyakov wanted it taken seriously. Craig wrote in his daybook that day, but accounts differ on whether he was in the room. Brecht, whose essay made the visit famous, is not recorded as speaking.

ties.note: Zhang directed both tours, the American in 1930 and the Soviet in 1935, and explained Mei's stage to foreign audiences.
Qi wrote many of Mei's new plays and planned the American tour with him for over a decade.
Eisenstein met him on arrival, wrote about him twice and filmed him on 29 March. Mei later wrote a chapter about their friendship.

Tretyakov was Brecht's Moscow friend and translator, and wrote to him in 1935. Reinhold Grimm argued that Tretyakov passed him the Formalist idea of making strange, but a manuscript study disputes that account.
Brecht watched Mei in Moscow and built his 'alienation effect' essay on the example. How much Mei's own practice matches Brecht's theory is still argued.
The two had staged the Moscow Art Theatre Hamlet together in 1911–12. In 1935 Craig was in the theatres and Stanislavsky stayed at home.
Co-founders of the Moscow Art Theatre in 1898. They had been estranged for years and in 1935 both were named to the reception committee.
Meyerhold staged Tretyakov's 'Roar, China!' in 1926. Both spoke on 14 April and both were killed in the purges, Tretyakov in 1937 and Meyerhold in 1940.
Eisenstein trained in Meyerhold's workshop in the early 1920s and called him his teacher. In 1939 he hid his teacher's archive at his dacha after the arrest.
They sailed and travelled together. Moscow crowds took the actress for Mei, the famous 'woman' of Chinese theatre.
Both saw the same New York run within weeks of each other, one for the Times and one in a private letter.
Yu's later account is one of two sources for what Stanislavsky said to Mei.

threads_out.note: The hosts of 1935 were caught in the terror two years later. Radek, who wrote on Mei in Izvestia, was a defendant at the January 1937 show trial. Tretyakov was arrested that July and killed, and Arosev of VOKS was shot in 1938. Meyerhold, arrested in 1939, was shot on 2 February 1940.

Eisenstein left Hollywood in late 1930, soon after hearing about Mei from Chaplin, for Mexico. There he met Diego Rivera and David Alfaro Siqueiros and planned 'Que viva México!' around the muralists' view of Mexican history.

Rabindranath Tagore met Mei in Beijing in May 1924, during the Indian poet's contested lecture tour of China, and saw him perform. Like Chaplin in 1930 and Eisenstein in 1935, he was a foreign artist of world fame who sought Mei out.

After Japanese forces took Shanghai and Nanjing in 1937, Mei withdrew to Hong Kong and later Shanghai. He grew a moustache to make it impossible to play women's roles and refused to perform under the occupation until 1945.
